paragraphs: Yelena won the first card game.

Darius accused her of hiding a card. Yelena invited him to count the deck. He did, discovered it was complete, and demanded another round on the grounds that knowing the deck was complete should surely improve his chances.
It did not.

Andrew sat on the arm of the couch and watched the second game fall apart while Akari took a photograph of Darius's expression. Nico leaned over Mara's shoulder to give advice nobody had asked for. Mara threatened to charge him for every suggestion.
At the projector, Sera folded her piece of cardboard twice and slid it under one of the rear feet. The picture on the wall straightened.
“Fixed,” she said.
Juno, sitting on the floor with his repaired headphones around his neck, looked over. “You can't call that a repair.”
“Why not?”
“The mount needs replacing.”
“The film needs ninety minutes,” Sera answered. “I expect the cardboard can manage that.”
Akari applauded. Juno pretended to be insulted and then offered to find a better piece of cardboard.

By the time they settled on a film, somebody had taken the cushions from two chairs to build a more comfortable place on the floor. Nico complained that his preferred film hadn't won, despite having changed his vote twice. Darius brought out the last of the bread and warned everyone that there would be no second dinner.

Andrew checked the wall clock. He had one route to confirm, a note to add to Juno's inspection report, and a short briefing to prepare for morning. He could have finished most of it before dinner. He could also finish it in ten minutes now.
He stayed for the first part of the film.

The hero, a man in an immaculate suit, was attempting to get through a kitchen window without being noticed. Nico insisted that the obvious solution was to break the glass. Sera pointed out that the entire point of the scene was not being noticed. Nico maintained that the glass should simply have been quieter.
Andrew laughed until his eyes watered.
Eventually he slipped away while the room was busy arguing about whether the hero had deserved to get caught.

His office was cool after the packed common room. He switched on the desk lamp, unfolded Mara's route sheet, and checked the approach one final time. The service road gave the patrol a little more room and a safer retreat. Juno's cold test had been scheduled and signed for; his machine would remain grounded if the inspection failed. Andrew made that note in the morning orders.
The room next door burst into laughter. Someone complained about the volume. Someone else made it louder.
Andrew looked down at the map. There was still more he could do. Another route to compare. Another possible failure to imagine. He had been very good at imagining failures since taking command.
He reached for his coffee, remembered the mug was empty, and set it aside.
A photograph was pinned to the wall beside his desk lamp.

Twelve young soldiers stood between two XR-17s, pressed together because Akari had insisted that everyone fit. The picture had been taken on a dry day. Their uniforms were less worn, and most of them were grinning at something outside the frame.

Matthias Adler stood at the back, taller than several of the others, with two fingers hooked into Andrew's collar. Andrew remembered trying to pull free just as Akari called for them to look at the camera. Matthias had laughed and refused to let go.
Andrew could no longer remember what the joke had been.
He straightened the corner of the photograph where it had curled from the wall and went back to the route sheet. He didn't need to study the picture to remember the faces.
A knock sounded at the door.
Darius stood in the corridor holding a small plate and a jar.
“Are you hiding?” he asked.
“Working.”
“I can see that. Are you hiding while you work?”
Andrew smiled. “Depends who you're asking.”

Darius came in and set the plate on the one corner of the desk not covered by paper. A bread roll lay on it, sliced and toasted. He unscrewed the little jar and spread a careful layer of jam all the way to the edges.
Andrew stared at the label.
“Strawberry? Where did you get that?”
“I have arrangements,” Darius said.
“With who?”
“People who appreciate bread.”
Andrew took a bite. The toast crackled, and for a few seconds the sweet taste occupied his attention completely.
“That's good,” he said.
“It's jam on bread.”
“Don't undersell your work.”
Darius leaned against the filing cabinet. He looked tired now, his apron gone and his sleeves rolled to the elbows.
“I wasn't happy about the pot,” he said.
“You had every right.”
“I know. I just don't want Juno thinking I'm going to hold it against him forever.”
“He doesn't. I think he wants to replace your entire kitchen.”
“Tell him to start with a pot.”
“I'll put it in writing.”
Darius smiled, then looked at the route sheet.
“You finished?”
“Almost.”
“How much is almost?”
Andrew glanced at the clock. “Ten minutes.”
“You told me ten minutes after breakfast.”
“That was a different ten minutes.”
“Of course.”
For a while Darius stayed where he was, not pressing. A cheer went up from the common room, followed by Nico loudly demanding that somebody replay the last scene.
Andrew looked at the map again. The route was marked. Mara had checked it. The inspection had a clear condition for approval. The morning briefing could be read without another hour of polishing.
He placed his pencil across the paper.
“If Nico picked the film after all, I'm blaming you.”
Darius pushed away from the cabinet. “Fair.”
Andrew picked up the plate and followed him back down the corridor.
A space had appeared on the couch beside Akari. She lifted her feet just long enough for him to sit and then laid them across his knees again.
“I charge for this,” Andrew told her.
“Put it on my account.”

On the wall, the man in the immaculate suit was now hanging from the kitchen window by his belt. Sera announced that they had reached the part of the story where everyone's advice would be useless. Nico protested that he had plenty of useful advice, and Mara told him that was precisely the problem.
Andrew settled back, the plate balanced on one hand.
Akari reached for his toast.
He caught her wrist without looking away from the film.
“Ask Darius.”
“I did,” she said. “He said you'd share.”
Across the room Darius was explaining the rules of a third card game to Yelena, who had already begun planning how to win it. He caught Andrew's expression and gave him a small, unrepentant shrug.
Andrew broke the toast in half.
Akari accepted her share, and the two of them watched the rest of the film with their friends.
